steps: The pressure of the gas inside the discharge tube is lowered so that there are fewer gas molecules in the path of the electrons.
The electrons can then travel a longer distance without colliding with gas molecules and gain sufficient energy to ionize them.
This makes the discharge and the production of cathode rays possible.
items.finalAnswer: The pressure is lowered so electrons can travel farther and gain enough energy to ionize gas molecules, producing cathode rays.

steps: According to the classical concept, an electron is a negatively charged particle that revolves around the nucleus in a definite path, like a planet revolving around the Sun.
With the development of modern atomic theory, electrons were found to have wave-like as well as particle-like properties.
It is now understood that an electron does not move in a precisely known fixed path; instead, its position is described in terms of the probability of finding it in a region around the nucleus.
items.finalAnswer: An electron was classically considered a particle moving in a definite path around the nucleus; modern theory describes its wave-particle nature and probability of position.

steps: The nuclei of radioactive elements have an unstable arrangement of protons and neutrons.
Their neutron-to-proton ratio is unsuitable for stability.
They emit radiation to change into more stable nuclei.
items.finalAnswer: Radioactive nuclei are unstable because their proton-neutron balance is unsuitable, so they emit radiation to become more stable.

steps: Scientists performed discharge tube experiments using different gases and electrodes.
Cathode rays showed the same properties and the same charge-to-mass ratio regardless of the gas or electrode used.
This showed that electrons are identical particles present in the atoms of all elements.
The positive particles observed in the experiments also led scientists to conclude that atoms contain protons; the hydrogen nucleus was identified as a proton.
Thus, electrons and protons are common constituents of the atoms of all elements.
items.finalAnswer: The same cathode-ray properties in experiments with different gases showed that identical electrons occur in all elements; experiments with positive rays established the presence of protons.

steps: A hydrogen atom has a small, positively charged nucleus containing one proton.
One negatively charged electron is present outside the nucleus.
The most common hydrogen atom, protium, has no neutron in its nucleus.
The electrostatic attraction between the proton and electron holds the atom together.
items.finalAnswer: A hydrogen atom consists of one proton in its nucleus and one electron outside it; ordinary hydrogen has no neutron.

steps: Radioactive isotopes emit energetic radiations, such as alpha particles, beta particles or gamma rays.
When this radiation passes through matter, it transfers energy to atoms and may remove electrons from them.
An atom that loses an electron becomes a positively charged ion; the removed electron is free.
items.finalAnswer: Radiation from a radioactive isotope can knock electrons out of atoms, forming positive ions and free electrons.

steps: Radioactivity is the spontaneous disintegration of an unstable atomic nucleus, accompanied by the emission of radiations.
Cobalt-60 is used in radiotherapy to treat cancer.
Iodine-131 is used to diagnose and treat disorders of the thyroid gland.
Carbon-14 is used to determine the age of ancient organic remains.
items.finalAnswer: Radioactivity is the spontaneous emission of radiation from unstable nuclei; radioactive isotopes are used in cancer treatment, thyroid diagnosis and treatment, and carbon dating.

steps: Required: Relative atomic mass of mercury.
Formula: Relative atomic mass = Σ(isotopic mass × relative abundance) ÷ Σ(relative abundances).
Result: The relative atomic mass of mercury is approximately 200.6; relative atomic mass has no unit.
